From 1:100. No more than seven positions are

index.t120: Hedging is mandatory, not netting. The algorithms are independent and may hold opposing positions on one instrument; on a netting account the second trade would close the first, and the result would diverge from the strategy. Execution is market; the instruments are ordinary: currency pairs, gold, indices, oil.
index.t122:
Return and drawdown
      scale together. A half multiplier gives half of both —
      it is a way to fit the risk to yourself. But remember: as you reduce
      the risk, raise the deposit according to the table above — otherwise some positions will go
      at the minimum lot with inflated risk, and the reduction will be illusory.
index.t123: On divergence of results. Copies open at current market prices, so your result will not match the strategy exactly — the difference accumulates from spread and slippage on every trade. At a flow of about 60 trades a month this is a noticeable amount, and the smaller the account, the larger it is in percentage terms. A deposit from $1,000 and a stable connection reduce the divergence; removing it entirely is impossible.
index.t125:
Two numbers are checked every week. Drawdown answers the question “how much
  does it hurt right now”; expectancy over the last 100 trades answers “is the system
  still working”. The actions are defined in advance, before things get unpleasant.
index.t126: Oversight is run by a separate watcher algorithm, not by a person acting on mood. It runs on the same server, reads the account history, recalculates every metric weekly — for the portfolio as a whole, for each of the two algorithms and for each instrument separately — and compares them against the thresholds in the table below. It separately reconciles the actual number of trades against the expected one: this is how a stopped or hung algorithm is detected, which would otherwise look simply like a prolonged drawdown.
index.t127:
The watcher makes no trading decisions
  and never intervenes in trades — it only measures and reports. Its logic
  has been checked against the full five-year history: the drawdown threshold was never reached,
  and the expectancy alarm fired twice — both times right at the boundary, and both times
  a review would have shown the system operating normally. On simulated deep
  drawdowns the warning arrives a month to six weeks before the critical level.

index.t144: The alarm threshold is expectancy below −0.05% per trade. The watcher checks against it once a week: across 254 weekly checks the alarm fired twice — on 28 Jan 2022 (−0.050%) and 6 Sep 2024 (−0.053%), both times right at the threshold. The average across all readings is +0.27%.
index.t145:
What happened next in both cases: the following hundred trades came out
  profitable, and expectancy returned to its average without any action at all.
  An alarm is not an order to stop but a demand to investigate: to check whether all
  algorithms are running, whether one has hung, whether the instruments have changed behaviour.
  Both times a review would have shown the system operating normally.
index.t146: The curve on the chart is continuous — it is recalculated after every trade rather than weekly, and it touched the threshold more often: 7 episodes over five years, the deepest at −0.132%. Only two of them survived to the day of the weekly check. We show this openly, so that a line beneath the threshold does not look like a contradiction of the text: the weekly control step is a deliberate choice, it damps out short spikes that there is nothing to be done about.
index.t147: There are deliberately no intermediate thresholds. Over five years expectancy fell to zero 17 times, and the following hundred trades after that were never once unprofitable — from +0.19% to +0.56% per trade against a historical average of +0.25%; in 11 cases out of 16, better than average. Reacting to such dips would mean trading against a reversion to the mean.
index.t148: Parameters are not changed during a drawdown. The settings were fitted on the entire available history of the instruments — six to seven years — while a drawdown is an event spanning a hundred trades. Changing parameters inside one means fitting the system to a random stretch.
